t.jose ignacio@-34.8,-54.6:
José Ignacio is a fishing village that fashion found, a scattering of low houses, sand lanes and a lighthouse on a small peninsula east of Punta del Este, where the Uruguayan coast turns wild. For decades it was a quiet place of fishermen and a few summer cottages, and some of that spirit remains in the unpaved streets, the old boats pulled up on the beach and the whitewashed church. Today it also has stylish restaurants and discreet hotels that draw visitors from Buenos Aires and São Paulo in summer, and it is quiet and nearly empty in winter.

The lighthouse, built in 1877, stands at the tip of the point, a white tower with a keeper's house, and the view from it takes in the Atlantic, the long beaches to either side and a line of surf. Offshore, whales can be seen between July and November, and sea lions haul out on the rocks. Just inland, Laguna Garzón is a shallow coastal lagoon bridged by a remarkable circular bridge, opened in 2015, which loops in a ring so that drivers slow down and enjoy the view of water and birds.

Riding here is a matter of long, flat coastal roads. Ruta 10 runs along the coast from Punta del Este toward La Paloma and Cabo Polonio, a narrow, sometimes rough two-lane with low dunes on one side and farmland on the other. The wind off the Atlantic is strong, and crosswinds can push a light bike around, so keep a firm grip. In summer, the road fills with holiday traffic, so aim for spring or autumn, when the sea is calm and the roads are quiet.

Fuel is the thing to plan: the nearest large town is San Carlos, about twenty-seven kilometres inland, and Maldonado and Punta del Este have plenty of stations. Fill the tank before heading east. Food is excellent, with fresh fish and grilled meat, and the local lamb is famous. In the evening, the sun goes down behind the land, but the sky over the sea glows. Wear layers, since the wind is cool even on warm days, and carry some local currency.
t.cabo polonio@-34.4,-53.8:
Cabo Polonio has no road. You leave the pavement of Ruta 10 at the park gate, park the bike, and either walk across the dunes or climb into a big four-wheel-drive truck for the ride across the sand, because vehicles of any ordinary kind are not allowed in. It is a small settlement of ramshackle houses perched on a rocky cape, with no mains electricity or running water, lit by candles, lanterns and a few solar panels, and it has a gloriously end-of-the-world feel. The sunsets here are said to be among the best in South America.

The cape juts into the Atlantic, with a lighthouse built in 1881 and a vast sea lion colony on the rocks beside it, thousands of animals barking, squabbling and basking. It is one of the largest in the region. Beyond the headland, the dunes stretch for miles, shifting with the wind, and the long beaches are empty of anything but the sound of surf. The place has a long history of shipwrecks and, in the past, of smugglers and sealers, and it has since become a favourite for artists, hippies and travellers.

For a motorcyclist, the practicalities are simple but important. Castillos, about twenty-four kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel, shops and a few places to eat, and the road from there to the park entrance is generally good. The sandy access track is closed to private vehicles, so you leave the bike at the car park and take the truck, which is part of the adventure. Check locally for weather and tides, because high seas can close beach routes.

Come with cash, a headlamp and warm clothes, since there are few places to charge or spend a card, and the nights can be cold even in summer. In January the settlement is packed with holidaymakers, and in winter it is almost empty. The nearby Santa Teresa National Park and the Laguna de Castillos offer woods, wetlands and birdlife, and are worth an extra day. Take your time, sleep to the sound of the sea, and walk the dunes at dawn.
t.kabul@34.5,69.2:
Kabul lies at about 1,800 metres, in a basin ringed by the bare, dun-coloured ridges of the Hindu Kush foothills, with the Kabul River slipping through the middle. It is one of the oldest cities in Central Asia, and has been a crossing point of empires for thousands of years. Babur, the founder of the Mughal dynasty, loved the place so much that he asked to be buried in a garden here, and Bagh-e Babur, on a slope on the south-west side of the city, was restored in the 2000s and remains a calm, terraced green space with a small mosque and a pavilion. The old citadel of Bala Hissar stands on a ridge above the city.

The weather is dry and bright, with hot summers and cold winters, and the air carries wood smoke and dust. The city is crowded, with traffic of every kind, markets, small workshops and the famous bird market at Ka Faroshi. The National Museum, badly damaged during the wars, has been partly restored and holds Bronze Age, Buddhist and Islamic pieces, and the Bamiyan region, a long day's drive to the west, was the site of the two great Buddhas destroyed in 2001.

The roads out of Kabul climb steeply. The route to Bamiyan leaves the capital westward, through the Maidan valley and then over the Unai Pass at over 3,000 metres, or via the Shibar Pass at about 2,700 metres, with dramatic gorges and hairpins. Surfaces vary from decent asphalt to broken sections and gravel, and weather can bring snow and landslides. Fuel is available in towns along the way but is limited, so top up in Kabul and carry spare. Travel conditions in Afghanistan are subject to serious security and political restrictions, and anyone thinking of travelling should consult current official advice and local contacts before making any plans.

Practically, Kabul has fuel stations, workshops and restaurants serving kebabs, rice dishes and strong green tea, and the markets are good places for dried fruit and nuts. Pace is slow on the outskirts, where trucks and donkey carts share the road. Dress modestly and respect local customs, and always ask before taking photographs. Leave early in the day, because the mountain roads are best driven in daylight.
t.kakrak valley caves including the niche:
The Kakrak Valley opens a few kilometres east of Bamiyan town, a side gorge cut into the same pale cliff that holds the famous niches, and it keeps a smaller sibling of the giants. Here, in a recess high in the rock, stood a Buddha of perhaps six metres, much smaller than the two colossi of the main valley but of the same period, and it too was damaged in 2001. The cliffs are riddled with caves, which were monks' cells, chapels and storerooms in the centuries when Bamiyan was a Buddhist monastic centre on the Silk Road, and some retain traces of painted ceilings.

The valley sits at about 2,500 metres in the central Hindu Kush, a high and dry landscape of ochre cliffs, green strips of poplar and wheat along the stream, and snow-capped peaks beyond. In the sixth and seventh centuries, Chinese pilgrims passed through, and one of them described gold and jewels on the big statues. Later research showed that some cave murals were painted in oil, centuries before the technique became known in Europe, which surprised art historians. The air is clear and thin, and the light on the rock is soft at dawn and dusk.

Reaching it is a journey. The road from Kabul crosses mountain passes of nearly three thousand metres, through gorges and past mud-brick villages, and reaches Bamiyan after a long day. Surfaces range from asphalt to broken stretches and gravel, with sudden weather changes in the mountains and the risk of landslides after heavy rain or snow. Any plan to travel in Afghanistan has to start with current official advice, since conditions and permissions change, and local knowledge is essential.

For practical matters, Bamiyan town, about two kilometres away, has simple guesthouses, small restaurants serving kebabs, bread and tea, and a bazaar. Fuel is limited and often more expensive than in Kabul, so carry extra on the road. Dress modestly and ask before photographing people. Bring layers, since nights are cold even in summer, and drink plenty of water to cope with the altitude. Walking in the valley means staying on marked paths, because unexploded munitions remain in some areas.
t.shahr i ghulghulah@34.8,67.8:
Shahr-i-Ghulghulah means the City of Screams, and the name carries a story. In 1221, according to the chronicles, Genghis Khan's army besieged the fortress that crowned this red clay hill above the Bamiyan valley, and his grandson Mutugen was killed in the fighting. The enraged Khan ordered the city destroyed and its people killed, and the ruins have borne the name ever since. Historians argue over the details, but the broken walls and towers on the summit are real, and the whole conical hill, about 1.7 kilometres from Bamiyan town, is a crumbling maze of mud brick.

From the top, the view takes in the entire valley, with the ochre cliff and its empty niches on one side and the green fields along the river below. The hill commanded the route between the Hindu Kush passes and Central Asia, and the fortress was in use from the early Islamic centuries until the Mongol destruction. The slopes are steep and unstable, and the paths are loose. UNESCO included the site in its 2003 listing of the cultural landscape and archaeological remains of the Bamiyan valley, alongside the Buddhist caves and the older fortress of Shahr-i-Zohak.

The journey to this valley is a serious one. The road from Kabul runs over passes at around 2,700 to over 3,000 metres, on surfaces that change from tarmac to rough gravel, and weather can bring snow or sudden rain. Any visit to Afghanistan requires careful reading of current official advice, and a rider would need local guidance, correct permissions and a realistic view of what is possible. The valley itself is quiet, and the mountain light at sunrise on the cliffs is unforgettable.

Practically, services are modest. Bamiyan town has a few guesthouses and restaurants serving kebabs, bread, rice and green tea, and a bazaar for supplies. Fuel is limited, so arrive with a full tank and carry extra. At 2,500 metres, the air is thin, and visitors may feel breathless on the climb up the hill, so go slowly and take water. Mines have been cleared from the main paths but not from every slope, so stay on tracks and follow local advice. Spring, with green fields and clear air, and early autumn are the best seasons.
t.cultural landscape and archaeological re:
The title of this stop is a UNESCO phrase, the Cultural Landscape and Archaeological Remains of the Bamiyan Valley, inscribed in 2003, and it covers more ground than most visitors expect. The Bamiyan valley is a long, narrow strip of green along a river, hemmed in by a high cliff of sandstone and conglomerate, and the listing takes in the Buddhist niches and caves, the ruined citadels of Shahr-i-Zohak and Shahr-i-Ghulghulah, the side valleys with their smaller shrines, and the monastic settlements that spread along the cliffs. In total, hundreds of caves were cut by monks between about the fifth and ninth centuries.

At the centre are the two niches that once held the colossal Buddhas, the larger about 55 metres tall and the smaller about 38, carved from the cliff and plastered, painted and gilded in antiquity. The Taliban destroyed them in March 2001, and the world was shocked. The empty recesses still tower above the valley, and international teams have since stabilised the rock and studied what remains, including fragments of the statues and wall paintings in the caves.

The valley's location explains its importance. It lies on a branch of the Silk Road where routes from India, Central Asia and Persia met, and the monks lived off pilgrims and merchants. Genghis Khan's army swept through in 1221, and the valley never fully recovered its former prominence. Today it is home to the Hazara people, who farm potatoes and wheat in terraces and keep sheep in the high pastures. The lakes of Band-e Amir, a chain of deep blue water, lie a few hours west.

Getting here from Kabul takes a long day on mountain roads with high passes, and surfaces vary from smooth to rough. Any travel plan needs up-to-date security advice, and conditions can change quickly. In the valley, cars and motorcycles are scarce, and the bazaar in Bamiyan town, about three kilometres off, is the place for tea, bread and supplies. Fuel is limited, so carry extra. Mornings are bright and cold, and the cliff glows orange as the sun climbs. Stay on cleared paths and respect local customs.
t.chuy@-33.7,-53.5:
Chuy is a town cut in half by a street, and the street is a border. On the Uruguayan side is Chuy, on the Brazilian side Chuí, and the dividing line runs along a wide avenue and a line of little stone markers, so that you can walk across the road to buy a coffee in another country. For the rider coming down the Atlantic coast of Uruguay, this is the end of the line, the far corner of the republic, with Brazil beyond and the great flat grasslands of the pampas stretching away in every direction.

The border gives the town its character. Duty-free shops line the main street on the Uruguayan side, selling electronics, perfume, wine and clothes to Brazilian shoppers, and the whole place has a market bustle that the sleepy coast road does not prepare you for. People speak Portuguese, Spanish, and a mixture of the two. If you plan to cross the line with a vehicle, bring your registration and insurance papers and do not take the paperwork lightly. Walking across to a restaurant for lunch is usually informal, but riding a motorcycle across is a different matter.

A few kilometres away stands the Fortaleza de Santa Teresa, a big stone fort begun by the Portuguese in the 1760s, taken by the Spanish, and fought over again. Its star-shaped walls sit on a rise among palms and grassland, with open lawns and long views over the lagoon country, and capybaras sometimes graze nearby. Just beyond is the Bañados del Este wetland reserve, a significant place for birds, with flamingos, herons and swans, and the Atlantic beach at Barra del Chuy, where wind and sand shape the coast.

The ride here follows Ruta 9, a long, straight, mostly well-surfaced road that runs through flat farmland and palm savannah, with little traffic outside the summer holidays. Wind is the main hazard: the Atlantic coast gets strong crosswinds, and a gust at the wrong moment can push a bike across the lane. Weather changes fast, with fog and rain possible even in summer. The best season is from November to March, though January is crowded.

Fuel is easy in Chuy, with several pumps along the main roads. Uruguay's fuel is not cheap, and you may find the Brazilian side is slightly different in price, but I would not stake a decision on it. Eat grilled meat and a plate of fish, finish a coffee, and watch the border traffic flow by.
t.punta del este@-35.0,-55.0:
Punta del Este is a long finger of rock and sand that juts into the South Atlantic, where the broad brown waters of the Río de la Plata meet the open ocean. For much of the year it is a quiet fishing and yachting town of about seven thousand permanent residents, and from late December to February it fills with Argentines, Brazilians and Uruguayans in search of sun, parties and sand. The peninsula divides two coasts: on one side is the Mansa, the calm, sheltered beach facing the river estuary, and on the other the Brava, where Atlantic swells roll in with real force.

The town has some unusual landmarks. On the Brava side, a huge sculpture of a hand rising from the sand, known as La Mano, was made by a Chilean artist in 1982 and has become the symbol of the resort. Farther west, along the coast road, stands Casapueblo, a white, sculpted building that looks half Greek island, half sandcastle, built over decades by the Uruguayan artist Carlos Páez Vilaró. Offshore lies Isla de Lobos, home to one of the biggest colonies of sea lions in the region, and boats make the trip from the harbour.

The riding starts after you leave. Ruta 10 runs east along the coast, past La Barra, José Ignacio and a series of beach towns, then continues through Rocha, a quiet province of lagoons, dunes and cattle ranches. The road is flat and mostly straight, with a good surface, and the wind blows steady off the ocean. Traffic is heavy in high summer and thin in other months. Cabo Polonio, the final destination, is a tiny village on a rocky point that has no electricity grid and can be reached only by a sandy track, usually by truck, and a seal colony sits on the rocks nearby.

Fuel is easy to find in Punta del Este and in Maldonado, a city of over fifty thousand a few kilometres inland, which also has supermarkets, banks and repair shops. Smaller towns along the coast have stations, but they can run short in peak season, so fill up when you can. Spanish helps, though many people here speak some English. Autumn and spring offer the best conditions, with mild weather and quiet roads, while winter brings cold, grey days and empty beaches.
